papers.title_in_file: Practicality of training a quantum-classical machine in the NISQ era
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, results, discussion (main text pp.1-8); appendices only skimmed
papers.what_it_is: An experimental study training a data re-uploading quantum classifier on an ion-trap processor with a genetic algorithm and with gradient-based optimizers.

assertions.value: The authors report that a genetic algorithm outperforms gradient-based approaches when run on noisy quantum hardware, reaching a training accuracy above 90% within nine generations with a population of 50.
quotes: We show that a genetic algorithm (GA), based on the concept of biological evolution, outperforms various gradient-based approaches when deployed on actual quantum hardware systems that are noisy.
Using a population size of only 50, a training accuracy exceeding 90% is achieved just within nine generations of the training routine.
assertions.certainty_reason: One ion-trap experiment on one binary classification task; empirical result.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is for one small task (250 training points) on one platform.

assertions.value: The authors train a data re-uploading quantum classifier for a binary classification problem on an ion-trap quantum processor, using 250 random points in a 2D plane, without the guidance of any classical simulation.
quotes: A set of 250 random data (points in a 2D plane) is chosen for the training procedure.
we introduce a binary classification problem and show the result of training conducted on a hybrid
a hybrid architecture that combines an ion trap-based quantum system with a classical processor.
without the guidance of any classical simulation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup, Section II, pp.2-3.

assertions.value: The authors state that their conclusion that GA optimizers surpass gradient-based optimizers in convergence rate and final accuracy holds under their problem setup using NISQ devices.
quotes: Empirical results from our comparative analysis clearly demonstrate that GA optimizers surpass gradient-based optimizers in terms of both convergence rate and final accuracy under our problem setup using NISQ devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper limits its own comparison to its problem setup, Section III, p.7.

assertions.value: The authors report that in noise-free simulation GA and BFGS are comparable in achievable accuracy and time to converge, and state that BFGS methods are only as good as GA if and only if the QPU is noiseless.
quotes: both GA and BFGS are comparable in terms of achievable accuracy and the time to converge but gradient descent shows slow convergence.
This indicates that BFGS methods are only as good as GA if and only if the QPU is noiseless.
assertions.certainty_reason: Inference from simulation plus one hardware experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The phrase 'if and only if' is an author inference from simulation, not a proof.

papers.what_it_is: A conceptual essay arguing that quantum neural networks should be defined through the Feynman path integral as representations of quantum amplitudes.

assertions.value: The author argues that the concept of a quantum neural network should be defined in terms of its most general function as a tool for representing the amplitude of an arbitrary quantum process.
quotes: We argue that the concept of a quantum neural network should be defined in terms of its most general function as a tool for representing the amplitude of an arbitrary quantum process.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's definitional argument; no experiment.

assertions.value: The author states that the field of quantum neural networks is the field of physics, not machine learning, and that the universe as a whole can be considered a quantum neural network.
quotes: The field of quantum neural networks is the field of physics not machine learning.
The universe as a whole can be considered as quantum neural network.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as the author's argued conclusions.

assertions.value: The author states that the path-integral amplitude expression formally coincides with the output of a two-layer approximating network when all output weights equal 1 and the transfer function is the exponent.
quotes: Expression (2) formally coincides with (3) if we put all the connection weights of the output neuron equal to 1 and choose exponent as transfer function.
It can be concluded that the output of a two-layer quantum neural network corresponds to the quantum amplitude of an arbitrary quantum process.
assertions.certainty_reason: A formal analogy argued in the text; no proof environment or experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The analogy is a re-description of the sum over paths; the paper gives no learning or computational result.

papers.title_in_file: What You Shouldn't Know About Quantum Computers
papers.partial_detail: foreword, contents, Myth 5 and Myth 6 chapters read closely; other chapters skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A popular book that corrects seven common myths about quantum computing.

assertions.value: The author reports that Gidney and Eker suggest 20 million physical qubits would be required to run Shor's algorithm against RSA-2048 using the best-known techniques and projected error rates.
quotes: Using the best-known techniques and projected error rates, Gidney and Eker suggest that 20 million physical qubits would be required.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited estimate in a popular book; the book spells the second author 'Eker'.
assertions.reader_inference: The source work is Gidney and Ekera (2021); verify against that paper, not this book.

assertions.value: The author states that if quantum computers start with roughly a hundred qubits and the number of qubits doubles every two years, it suggests that in about 34 years (around 2058) they could crack even the most robust RSA encryption standards.
quotes: If we start with roughly a hundred qubits today, and the number of qubits doubles every two years, it suggests that in about 34 years (around 2058), quantum computers could become powerful enough to crack even the most robust RSA encryption standards.
assertions.certainty_reason: An illustrative extrapolation, not a result.
assertions.reader_inference: The extrapolation treats physical qubit count as the only limit.

assertions.value: The author states that whether quantum computers differ from classical computers is not known; the questions of P versus NP and of NP in BQP have no mathematical proof, though the author suspects the answer to both is no.
quotes: We don't really know if quantum computers are any different from classical computers, but we highly suspect they are.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author's statement about open complexity questions in a popular book.

assertions.value: The author states that, for brevity, the book does not add all the necessary caveats to statements about complexity as if it were a graduate class in computer science.
quotes: In this book, for brevity, I won't add all the necessary caveats to statements about complexity as if it were a graduate class in computer science.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book states its own limit, Myth 5, p.98.

papers.title_in_file: Towards molecular docking with neutral atoms
papers.partial_detail: full main text read from abstract to conclusions
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study mapping molecular docking to a maximum-weight independent set problem on a neutral-atom processor, solved with a variational quantum adiabatic algorithm and a graph neural network that predicts the parameters.

assertions.value: The authors state that their developed proof of concept demonstrates the feasibility of solving the molecular docking problem using neutral atoms.
quotes: In this work, the developed proof of concept demonstrates the feasibility of solving the molecular docking problem using neutral atoms.
assertions.certainty_reason: A small simulated proof of concept; the authors' own claim of feasibility.
assertions.reader_inference: The proof of concept uses two small molecules and a simulator, not hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that they simulate neutral atom devices with Pulser and that, given computational limitations, they were not able to compare a full molecular docking problem in a real-world application with their methods.
quotes: With Pulser we can simulate the behavior of neutral atom devices.
Given our computational limitations, we were not able to compare a full molecular docking problem in a real-world application with our methods.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit in Section 12, p.15.

assertions.value: The authors report that the prediction errors of the machine-learning parameter models are not particularly good, but that the MLQAA results are only slightly below those of VQAA at 10 rounds.
quotes: Objectively, these values are not particularly good, especially considering the impact of a small error on performance, particularly in cases with significant spacing between qubits.
the MLQAA results are only slightly below those of VQAA at 10 rounds.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one small simulated data set; Table 1 holds the numeric errors.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper itself says the number and variety of graphs are insufficient for quality training.

assertions.value: The authors state that the current implementation bottleneck lies in embedding the problem into the register, presenting several challenges.
quotes: However, the current implementation bottleneck lies in embedding the problem into the register, presenting several challenges.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit, Section 13, p.16.

papers.title_in_file: Hybrid quantum transfer learning for crack image classification on NISQ hardware
papers.what_it_is: An application paper that adds a quantum circuit to a pretrained ResNet18 for crack classification and runs it on simulators and IBM hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that their experiments show classification of crack images is achievable on current NISQ hardware, with similar results on simulators and IBM superconducting quantum computers.
quotes: Nevertheless, our experiments show that the classification of crack images is indeed achievable even on the current NISQ hardware.
In general, we achieved similar results on PennyLane's and IBM's simulators and IBM's superconducting quantum computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on one dataset; accuracy numbers are in Table 5.

assertions.value: The authors report that on ibmq_lima the actual execution time was 4 hours, only about 4% of the total training time, and that a classical deep learning approach would need only 3 hours for 100 epochs of training.
quotes: The actual execution time on ibmq_lima was 4 hours, so only about 4% of the total training time.
In comparison, a classical deep learning approach would only need 3 hours for 100 epochs of training.
assertions.certainty_reason: One backend, one dataset; queue times vary.

assertions.value: The authors use 1,223 image patches (723 with cracks and 500 without) and a quantum transfer learning model with a pretrained ResNet18 whose features are reduced from 512 to 4 before the quantum circuit.
quotes: We used 1,223 patches as our complete dataset, 723 patches with cracks and 500 without cracks.
As classical algorithm, we use a ResNet18 network
we decided to reduce from 512 features to 4 features in the first linear layer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup, Sections 4 and 5.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that backpropagation is not available on real devices, so finite-difference or parameter-shift gradients are used, with a larger number of evaluations, longer training times and more jobs to submit as the consequences.
quotes: At the moment, backpropagation is not available on real devices.
A larger number of evaluations, longer training times, and more jobs to submit are the consequences.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit in Section 7, p.9.

papers.title_in_file: Advantages of multistage quantum walks over QAOA
papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation study comparing multistage quantum walks with QAOA for Ising ground-state problems.

assertions.value: The authors state that using numerical and analytical methods they obtain evidence that multistage quantum walks outperform QAOA with equivalent resources.
quotes: Using both numerical and analytical methods, we obtain evidence that MSQW outperforms QAOA, using equivalent resources.
we gave analytical evidence that MSQWs outperform QAOA for approximating quantum annealing, i.e., with the same number of stages we obtain a smaller error.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation on small spin-glass instances plus analysis; described by the authors as evidence.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper compares against QAOA only, not against the best classical solvers.

assertions.value: The authors state that the numerical comparisons cover small stage numbers, with p = 1, p = 2 and p = 5, and that the analytical results suggest MSQW is better if the protocols can be applied for many stages.
quotes: We have therefore carried out detailed numerical comparisons for small values of p, starting with p = 1, and continuing with p = 2 and p = 5.
strongly suggest that MSQW simulate quantum annealing schedules better than QAOA for the same resources, if we can apply these protocols for many stages.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its numerics in Section V.

assertions.value: The authors report that, with their heuristic parameters, the multistage quantum walk success probability reaches values as high as 0.8 for a wide region of parameters (Fig. 5b).
quotes: which reaches values as high as 0.8 for a wide region of parameters (Fig. 5b).
assertions.certainty_reason: One simulated instance family; empirical.

assertions.value: The authors state that analysing other optimization problems such as MaxCUT or Maximum Independent set, and a comparison to the best-known classical algorithms, is future work and would be crucial to understand the potential of the approach.
quotes: Future work analysing the performance of MSQWs for other optimization problems of interest (such as MaxCUT or Maximum Independent set), as well as a comparison to the best-known classical algorithms, would be crucial to truly understand the potential of this approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit, Section VII.

papers.title_in_file: Understanding quantum machine learning also requires rethinking generalization
papers.what_it_is: A study using randomization tests and two theorems to show that quantum neural networks can fit random labels and random quantum states, so uniform generalization bounds cannot explain their generalization.

assertions.value: The authors report that state-of-the-art quantum neural networks accurately fit random states and random labeling of training data.
quotes: Our experiments reveal that state-of-the-art quantum neural networks accurately fit random states and random labeling of training data.
Existing QML models can accurately fit random labels to quantum states.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical experiments on tested qubit numbers and training sizes.

assertions.value: The paper proves that, for quantum states fulfilling its distinguishability condition, a parameterized quantum circuit of polynomial depth can produce any labeling of the states.
quotes: With Theorem 2, we understand that PQCs can produce any labeling of arbitrary sets of quantum states, provided they fulfill our distinguishability condition.
Notice that Definition 1 is needed for the correctness of Theorem 2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2 (finite sample expressivity of PQCs), Section II.E, p.9; proof in Appendix B (not checked).

assertions.value: The authors state that their empirical findings are restricted to the number of qubits and training samples tested, and that their results do not preclude the possibility of good generalization with few training data.
quotes: Our empirical findings are restricted to the number of qubits and training samples we tested.
Our results do not preclude the possibility of good generalization with few training data
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit, Section II.E.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Algorithm for Testing Graph Completeness
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, Sections 2-3 and conclusions; appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that proposes a Szegedy quantum walk plus quantum phase estimation algorithm to test whether a graph is complete.

assertions.value: The authors state that the time complexity of their algorithm is O(log2 n), where n is the number of nodes of the graph, and describe it as a clear quantum advantage over classical methods.
quotes: The time complexity of our algorithm is O(log2 n), where n is the number of nodes of the graph.
Consequently, the complexity is O(log2 n), polylogarithmic in n.
assertions.certainty_reason: Analytical complexity claim; the paper treats the controlled walk operators as efficient and gives no experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The bound depends on the assumption that the controlled walk operator is efficient, and on input access to the adjacency matrix.

assertions.value: The authors state that a classical check of all links takes O(n2) steps and that the classical eigenvalue QR algorithm has complexity O(n3), and use these as comparison points.
quotes: To compare the complexity of our algorithm with a classical one, we consider the number of steps required to check all the links in a graph G, which is O(n2).
the classical eigenvalue QR algorithm [30, 31] which complexity O(n3)
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' choice of baselines.
assertions.reader_inference: A Grover-style search is also discussed by the authors, so the baseline choice shapes the advantage claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that a Grover search with an oracle that highlights missing links would give a complexity O(n), and that their algorithm does not use such an oracle and is not searching for marked elements.
quotes: For example, a Grover search might include an oracle that can highlight missing links in the incomplete graph and then identify them by a Grover search, leading to a complexity O(n).
In our algorithm, we do not use such an oracle and we are not searching for marked elements either.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' comparison; not derived in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a complete graph, specifying the number of marked nodes ensures a bounded running time that tends to a constant value of three time steps for large n and m.
quotes: ensures a bounded running time, which tends to a constant value of three time steps for large
assertions.certainty_reason: Introduction statement; the derivation in Section 2.5 and the appendices was not checked.
